subject: History & Civics
text: What is the quorum of the Lok Sabha? What happens when quorum is not present?
modelAnswer: Quorum of Lok Sabha: 1/10th of the total membership = 55 members (out of 550). If quorum is not present, the Speaker must either adjourn the House or suspend the sitting until quorum is present. No valid business can be conducted without quorum.
keyPoints: Quorum = 1/10 of total membership (55 for Lok Sabha)
Without quorum: Speaker adjourns or suspends the sitting
Quorum ensures minimum attendance for valid legislative business

subject: History & Civics
text: Explain the discretionary power of the Governor to invite a leader to form government when there is no clear majority (hung assembly).
modelAnswer: When no party wins a clear majority (hung assembly), the Governor exercises discretionary power: (a) The Governor assesses which party/coalition is most likely to command majority support and invites that leader to form government and prove majority within specified time. (b) The Governor can use personal judgment in selecting who gets the first chance — typically the single largest party is invited first. This is the Governor's most significant discretionary function.
keyPoints: Hung assembly: no party with clear majority
Governor's discretion: invite single largest party/likely majority leader
Leader must prove majority on floor of House within specified period

subject: History & Civics
text: Explain: (a) What is judicial review? (b) What is the significance of the writ of Habeas Corpus?
modelAnswer: (a) Judicial review: the power of the courts (Supreme Court and High Courts) to examine the constitutionality of laws passed by Parliament/state legislatures and executive orders. If found unconstitutional (violating fundamental rights or constitution), the court can declare them null and void. It protects the constitution's supremacy. (b) Habeas Corpus: 'You shall have the body' — a writ issued by a court directing any person holding another person in custody to produce the detainee before the court. It protects against illegal detention and arbitrary arrest; ensures personal liberty.
keyPoints: Judicial review: courts examine constitutionality of laws; can declare them void
Habeas Corpus: order to produce detained person before court
Habeas Corpus protects personal liberty from illegal/arbitrary detention

subject: History & Civics
text: What were the objectives of the Indian National Army (INA) formed under Subhas Chandra Bose?
modelAnswer: The Indian National Army (INA) was formed in 1942 with the main objectives: (a) To liberate India from British rule by military force, fighting alongside Japanese forces in Southeast Asia. (b) To organize Indian prisoners of war and Indian immigrants in Southeast Asia into an armed force against the British. (c) Its motto was 'Unity, Faith and Sacrifice' and slogan was 'Jai Hind'. Bose called for 'Give me blood, I will give you freedom'.
keyPoints: INA objective: liberate India by military means alongside Japan
Organized Indian POWs in Southeast Asia
Motto: Unity, Faith, Sacrifice; Slogan: Jai Hind; Bose = Netaji

subject: History & Civics
text: What was the contribution of Raja Rammohan Roy to the abolition of Sati? State the year it was abolished.
modelAnswer: Raja Rammohan Roy (founder of Brahmo Samaj) campaigned vigorously against the inhuman practice of Sati — burning of Hindu widows on the funeral pyres of their husbands. He wrote against it, petitioned the British Government, and mobilized public opinion. His persistent efforts led Governor General William Bentinck to pass the Bengal Sati Regulation Act in 1829, declaring Sati illegal and punishable as culpable homicide.
keyPoints: Raja Rammohan Roy: founder of Brahmo Samaj; campaigned against Sati
Lobbied British Government; wrote and petitioned against the practice
Sati abolished 1829 (Bengal Sati Regulation Act) under Bentinck

subject: History & Civics
text: What is an Adjournment Motion? When can it be moved in the Lok Sabha?
modelAnswer: Adjournment Motion: a motion to adjourn all other business of the House and draw immediate attention to a definite matter of urgent public importance that has occurred recently. It is a device to criticize the government for a specific recent failure or emergency. Conditions: (a) Must relate to a definite, recent matter of urgent public importance. (b) Must receive support of at least 50 members. (c) The Speaker's permission is required. (d) Cannot be about a matter sub judice.
keyPoints: Adjournment Motion: to discuss urgent recent matter of public importance
Requires support of 50+ members; Speaker's permission needed
Used to criticize government; cannot be about sub judice matter

subject: History & Civics
text: Distinguish between National Emergency (Article 352), President's Rule (Article 356) and Financial Emergency (Article 360) with reference to their grounds.
modelAnswer: National Emergency (Art. 352): proclaimed when the security of India is threatened by war, external aggression, or armed rebellion. Covers the whole or part of India. President's Rule (Art. 356): proclaimed when the constitutional machinery of a state fails — state government cannot be carried on in accordance with provisions of the Constitution. Operates in a specific state. Financial Emergency (Art. 360): proclaimed when the financial stability or credit of India or any part is threatened. Financial Emergency has never been declared in India.
keyPoints: Art.352 (National): war/external aggression/armed rebellion → national security
Art.356 (President's Rule): constitutional breakdown in a state
Art.360 (Financial): financial stability/credit threatened; never used

subject: History & Civics
text: What was the Swadeshi Movement? Name any two methods used in the movement.
modelAnswer: Swadeshi Movement (1905): launched in response to Lord Curzon's partition of Bengal. It aimed to promote Indian-made goods (swadeshi = of own country) and boycott British-made goods. Methods: (a) Boycott of British goods — burning foreign cloth, refusing to buy imported goods. (b) Promoting indigenous (Indian-made) industries and goods. (c) Use of vernacular languages; (d) National education movement; (e) Passive resistance and public meetings.
keyPoints: Swadeshi: promote Indian goods; launched after Bengal partition (1905)
Methods: boycott of British goods, burning foreign cloth
Also: promoting Indian industries, national education, public meetings

subject: History & Civics
text: What is the Budget Session of Parliament? State its importance.
modelAnswer: Budget Session: the most important session of Parliament, held from February to May. The Union Budget (Annual Financial Statement) is presented by the Finance Minister, usually on February 1st. Importance: (a) Parliament scrutinizes and approves the government's income and expenditure plans for the next financial year. (b) Demand for Grants are voted. (c) Finance Bill (tax proposals) is passed. (d) It ensures parliamentary control over public finances.
keyPoints: Budget Session: Feb–May; Finance Minister presents Union Budget (Feb 1)
Parliament approves income & expenditure plans for next FY
Finance Bill passed; Demand for Grants voted; controls public finances

subject: History & Civics
text: Explain the original jurisdiction of the Supreme Court of India.
modelAnswer: Original jurisdiction (Article 131): The Supreme Court has exclusive original jurisdiction (first court to hear) in disputes between: (a) The Union and one or more states. (b) The Union and states on one side versus other states on other side. (c) Two or more states. These disputes must involve questions of law or fact on which the existence or extent of a legal right depends. The SC has special original jurisdiction in Fundamental Rights (Article 32) — citizens can approach it directly.
keyPoints: Original jurisdiction: disputes between Union and States, or between States
Article 131: exclusive original jurisdiction (no other court can hear these)
Also Art. 32: direct petition to SC for Fundamental Rights enforcement

subject: History & Civics
text: What was the Sarajevo Crisis? How did it trigger the First World War?
modelAnswer: Sarajevo Crisis (1914): Archduke Franz Ferdinand, heir to the Austro-Hungarian throne, and his wife were assassinated in Sarajevo, Bosnia, by Gavrilo Princip (a Bosnian Serb nationalist) on 28 June 1914. Impact: Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia and issued an ultimatum. Serbia's partial acceptance was rejected, leading Austria-Hungary to declare war on Serbia. The alliance system (Triple Alliance vs Triple Entente) drew in other nations: Russia mobilized for Serbia; Germany declared war on Russia and France; Germany invaded Belgium, bringing Britain into the war — World War I began.
keyPoints: Assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand (28 June 1914) in Sarajevo
Austria-Hungary blamed Serbia; issued ultimatum; declared war
Alliance system: Russia defended Serbia → Germany vs Russia+France; UK joined when Belgium invaded

subject: History & Civics
text: What was the Doctrine of Lapse? Name any two states annexed under it.
modelAnswer: Doctrine of Lapse: a policy introduced by Lord Dalhousie (1848-1856) whereby if a native ruler died without a natural male heir, the state would be annexed ('lapse') to the British East India Company. Adopted children were not recognized as legal heirs for succession. States annexed: (a) Satara (1848), (b) Jhansi (1853), (c) Nagpur (1854), (d) Awadh (1856) — though Awadh was on different grounds (mismanagement).
keyPoints: Doctrine of Lapse: Dalhousie's policy; state annexed if ruler dies without natural heir
Adopted sons not recognized as heirs for succession
States annexed: Satara, Jhansi, Nagpur (and Awadh)

subject: History & Civics
text: State the composition and functions of the Security Council of the United Nations.
modelAnswer: Composition: 15 members — 5 permanent (P5: USA, UK, France, Russia, China) and 10 non-permanent elected for 2-year terms by General Assembly. Functions: (a) Primary responsibility for maintenance of international peace and security. (b) Can impose sanctions and authorize use of force against aggressors. (c) Recommends admission of new UN members. (d) Can establish peacekeeping operations. (e) Recommends candidates for Secretary General. Special power: P5 have veto power — any P5 member can block any substantive resolution.
keyPoints: 15 members: 5 permanent (P5) + 10 non-permanent (2-year terms)
Primary responsibility: international peace and security
P5 veto power: any permanent member can block resolutions

subject: History & Civics
text: What are Money Bills? How do they differ from ordinary bills in the legislative process?
modelAnswer: Money Bills: Bills dealing exclusively with taxation, government expenditure, borrowing, or related financial matters (defined under Article 110). They can only originate in the Lok Sabha, not in Rajya Sabha. Difference: Ordinary bills: must be passed by both Houses with equal powers; deadlock resolved by joint sitting. Money bills: introduced only in Lok Sabha (Speaker certifies it as Money Bill). Rajya Sabha can only make recommendations within 14 days — Lok Sabha can accept or reject them. President cannot withhold assent from a Money Bill (after Lok Sabha passes it).
keyPoints: Money Bill: only taxation, expenditure, borrowing (Article 110)
Introduced only in Lok Sabha; Speaker certifies
Rajya Sabha can only recommend changes; Lok Sabha can ignore them

subject: History & Civics
text: Describe the significance of the Lucknow Pact (1916) and explain how it fostered Hindu-Muslim unity.
modelAnswer: Lucknow Pact (1916): a historic agreement between the Indian National Congress (led by Bal Gangadhar Tilak) and the Muslim League (led by Muhammad Ali Jinnah). Significance: (a) Congress recognized separate electorates for Muslims — concession for Hindu-Muslim unity. (b) Both organizations jointly demanded self-government (Swaraj) for India. (c) Ended the Moderate-Extremist divide in Congress (reunification after Surat Split). (d) It was the first major instance of Hindu-Muslim political cooperation against British rule. (e) Showed a united front — weakened the British policy of 'divide and rule'.
keyPoints: Lucknow Pact 1916: INC + Muslim League agreement; Tilak + Jinnah
Congress accepted separate electorates for Muslims (controversial compromise)
Both demanded self-government; ended Moderate-Extremist divide; undermined 'divide and rule'

subject: History & Civics
text: Explain the role of Swami Vivekananda in the Indian National Movement and social reform.
modelAnswer: Swami Vivekananda (1863-1902): (a) Religious/social reform: Represented a revitalized Hinduism at the Parliament of World Religions, Chicago (1893) — boosted Indian self-confidence and pride. Founded Ramakrishna Mission (1897) for social service. (b) Nationalism: preached 'Be proud of India's heritage; awaken to serve the motherland'. His teachings inspired Tilak, Aurobindo and other national leaders. (c) Social reform: emphasized service to the poor as service to God, attacked caste discrimination and untouchability.
keyPoints: Chicago Parliament of Religions 1893: boosted Indian self-confidence
Founded Ramakrishna Mission 1897: social service organization
Inspired nationalism; attacked caste discrimination; 'serve the poor = serve God'

subject: History & Civics
text: What is meant by 'judicial independence'? State any two provisions in the Indian Constitution that ensure independence of the judiciary.
modelAnswer: Judicial independence: the principle that judges must be free from political pressure, executive interference, or any other influence so they can deliver impartial justice based solely on law and facts. Constitutional provisions: (a) Security of tenure — Supreme Court judges cannot be removed except by an address of both Houses of Parliament with special majority (very difficult). (b) Fixed service conditions — salaries of judges are charged to Consolidated Fund of India, not subject to Parliamentary vote, preventing financial pressure. (c) Prohibition on practice after retirement in courts where they served.
keyPoints: Judicial independence: free from political/executive interference
Security of tenure: removal needs special majority of both Houses
Salaries from Consolidated Fund: not subject to Parliamentary vote

subject: History & Civics
text: State any three consequences of World War II.
modelAnswer: (a) Formation of United Nations (1945): to maintain international peace and prevent future wars. (b) Emergence of two Superpowers (USA and USSR) leading to the Cold War — division of world into two ideological blocs. (c) Decolonization: decline of European empires; Asian and African countries gained independence — India (1947), etc. (d) Marshall Plan: USA helped rebuild war-devastated Europe, creating dependency and influence. (e) Nuclear age: atomic bombing of Hiroshima and Nagasaki showed devastating power; nuclear arms race began. (f) Partition of Germany into East and West.
keyPoints: UN formed 1945 to maintain international peace
USA-USSR superpowers → Cold War (two ideological blocs)
Decolonization: Asian/African independence (India 1947); nuclear age began

subject: History & Civics
text: What was the Subsidiary Alliance system introduced by Lord Wellesley? What were its effects on Indian states?
modelAnswer: Subsidiary Alliance (Lord Wellesley, 1798): under this system, Indian rulers had to: (a) Maintain a British military contingent in their territory paid for by the ruler (or give territory in lieu). (b) Accept a British Resident at their court. (c) Not employ any European not approved by the British. (d) Not enter foreign relations without British consent. Effects: (a) Indian rulers lost military power and diplomatic sovereignty. (b) British troops were stationed across India, strengthening British control. (c) Indian states became subsidiary (subordinate) to the British. States like Hyderabad, Mysore, Awadh, Maratha states were brought under this system.
keyPoints: Subsidiary Alliance: Wellesley 1798; rulers host/pay British troops
Rulers accept British Resident; cannot have independent foreign relations
Effect: rulers lost military and diplomatic independence; British dominant

subject: History & Civics
text: Explain the procedure for removal of the Speaker of the Lok Sabha.
modelAnswer: The Speaker of Lok Sabha can be removed by a resolution passed by an effective majority (majority of all then members of the House — absolute majority, not simple majority) under Article 94. Procedure: (a) A 14-day prior notice must be given before moving the resolution for removal. (b) During the pendency of a resolution for his removal, the Speaker may not preside over the sitting but may vote in the first instance. (c) The resolution must be passed by majority of total membership of Lok Sabha. This high threshold protects the Speaker's independence.
keyPoints: Speaker removed by effective majority (absolute majority of total members)
14-day prior notice required before moving removal resolution
Speaker may not preside but can vote during pendency of resolution

subject: History & Civics
text: State the objectives of the United Nations as laid down in its Charter.
modelAnswer: The main objectives/purposes of the UN (Article 1 of UN Charter): (a) To maintain international peace and security by taking effective collective measures. (b) To develop friendly relations among nations based on respect for equal rights and self-determination of peoples. (c) To achieve international co-operation in solving economic, social, cultural, or humanitarian problems and promoting respect for human rights. (d) To be a centre for harmonising nations' actions in attaining these common ends.
keyPoints: Maintain international peace and security (collective measures)
Develop friendly relations; self-determination of peoples
International cooperation: economic, social, cultural; promote human rights

subject: History & Civics
text: What was the Rowlatt Act (1919)? Why did it provoke widespread opposition?
modelAnswer: Rowlatt Act (1919): also called the 'Black Act'. It gave the British Government power to arrest and imprison any person without trial or charge for up to 2 years and try persons by a Special Tribunal without jury. Opposition: (a) It took away the fundamental right to liberty and right to a fair trial. (b) It was seen as an extension of wartime repressive laws into peacetime. (c) Gandhi called it 'lawless law' and launched the Satyagraha against it. (d) Led to the Jallianwala Bagh Massacre (13 April 1919) when peaceful protesters were fired upon.
keyPoints: Rowlatt Act 1919 (Black Act): imprisonment without trial for 2 years
Denied right to fair trial; emergency wartime measures extended to peace
Gandhi's Satyagraha against it; led to Jallianwala Bagh massacre

subject: History & Civics
text: Why is 1857 considered a turning point in India's relationship with Britain? State two major changes after 1857.
modelAnswer: 1857 was the first major organized armed uprising against British rule (the Sepoy Mutiny or First War of Independence). It showed Indians' dissatisfaction with British rule and the potential for resistance. Changes after 1857: (a) Government of India Act 1858: rule of East India Company ended; the Crown (British Parliament) directly took control. India came directly under Queen Victoria. (b) The British Indian Army was reorganized — Indian soldiers were reduced in proportion; European troops increased. Artillery placed under Europeans. (c) Policy of divide and rule was intensified — communal divisions exploited. (d) Policy of non-interference in social/religious affairs was announced.
keyPoints: 1857 uprising ended East India Company rule; Crown took over (Act 1858)
Army reorganized: fewer Indian soldiers, more Europeans in key positions
Policy of divide and rule intensified; non-interference in social affairs declared

subject: History & Civics
text: Distinguish between the nominal and real executive in India. Who is the real executive?
modelAnswer: Nominal executive (President): The President is the constitutional/formal head. In theory, all executive power is vested in the President. In practice, the President acts on the advice of the Council of Ministers and does not exercise power independently. Real executive (Prime Minister and Council of Ministers): The Prime Minister is the head of the real executive. The Cabinet, collectively responsible to the Lok Sabha, makes actual policy decisions and governs. The President is a rubber stamp who gives formal approval. India follows a Parliamentary (Westminster) system — real power lies with elected representatives.
keyPoints: Nominal executive: President (formal head; acts on Cabinet advice)
Real executive: Prime Minister + Council of Ministers (collective responsibility)
India: Parliamentary system; President is constitutional head, PM wields real power

subject: History & Civics
text: Name any four writs issued by the Supreme Court and High Courts for enforcement of Fundamental Rights. Briefly explain one.
modelAnswer: The five writs (Article 32 for SC, Article 226 for HC): (a) Habeas Corpus, (b) Mandamus, (c) Prohibition, (d) Quo Warranto, (e) Certiorari. Mandamus: 'We command' — issued to a public official, authority, tribunal, or government body commanding it to perform a duty it is legally bound to perform but has refused or neglected to do. Example: if a public authority refuses to issue a licence it is required to issue by law, court issues Mandamus.
keyPoints: Five writs: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Quo Warranto, Certiorari
Mandamus: command to perform a legally required duty (cure neglect)
Habeas Corpus: produce detainee before court (protect liberty)
